english_comparison.source: Unchanged pointed MT, first hearing infinitive; second איש plus participle; rebuke/wise man singular, fools plural.
english_comparison.context: 7:4 wise hearts/mourning versus fools/joy; 7:6 foolish laughter likened to crackling thorns.
english_comparison.policy: Original-language fidelity and meaningful patterns before fluency; understandable modern English; no invented distinct listeners or theology.

candidates.A: It is better to hear the rebuke of a wise man than to hear the song of fools.
candidates.B: It is better to hear the rebuke of a wise man than for a man to hear the song of fools.
candidates.C: It is better to hear a wise man’s rebuke than to be a man listening to fools’ song.

english_comparison.actual_assessment:
A conveys the central contrast accurately: a wise person’s rebuke is preferable to fools’ song. It retains the singular wise man and plural fools, with no unsupported distinct listeners. Its main loss is structural: it replaces the source’s second “man hearing” with another infinitive, making the two halves more symmetrical than the Hebrew.

B also conveys that contrast accurately and retains an explicit generic “man” in the second half. “For a man to hear” does not require a different listener from whoever hears the rebuke; both can describe anyone facing the alternatives. Nevertheless, the English asymmetry can momentarily suggest a change of subject. B preserves the explicit participant, although it recasts the Hebrew noun-plus-participle construction as an infinitival clause.

C preserves an explicit man engaged in listening, but “to be a man listening” introduces an emphasis on being that kind of person. This is a possible interpretation of the source’s comparison with “a man hearing,” yet it makes the activity-versus-person contrast more conspicuous than necessary. The phrasing is also cumbersome. “Fools’ song” is understandable, though less natural here than “the song of fools.”

The explicit איש contributes a stated generic human participant and a grammatical asymmetry. It does not, on the supplied evidence, establish a second, distinct hearer or a special contrast involving masculinity. A preserves the practical meaning of that generic participant through its understood hearer, but not its explicit expression.

The neighboring contrasts favor the proverb’s sharp opposition between receiving wise correction and enjoying foolish entertainment. A delivers that opposition most crisply; B retains more of the verse’s uneven expression without materially obscuring it.

Under the stated priority of source patterns before fluency, I narrowly prefer B, with A a strong alternative that reads more naturally while smoothing a real structural feature. C makes a less economical interpretive choice. This preference does not establish uniquely optimal English or any claim about the priority of alternative Hebrew texts.
english_comparison.tradeoff: B makes MT's generic listener visible but is less crisp than A; C foregrounds being that kind of person. Do not infer different doctrine, two people or priority from the English preference.
